p.x:
For my birthday, my uncle gave me a small camera. Now I take photos everywhere! My favourite time is the evening, when the sunset makes the sky orange and pink. It's so pretty.
Last weekend, I took photos of my family in the park. My little sister kept moving, so I said, "Stand still for a moment!" Then my dad blinked in every photo. We laughed a lot.
I also like taking photos of shadows. In the evening, our shadows are very long and funny. When I have good photos, I print them and put them on my bedroom wall.

You don't need an expensive camera to take good photos; a phone is enough. Here are some tips.
First, check the focus. If you move, your photo will be blurry. Hold your phone with two hands, or use a tripod for night photos. A sharp photo always looks better.
Second, think about the background. A busy background can spoil a photo. Try a different angle: stand higher, or get closer for a close-up. You can also put something interesting in the foreground, like flowers, to give the picture depth.
Third, use natural lighting. Avoid the flash when possible; it makes faces look flat. Don't zoom too much, because the photo may lose quality and you'll see the pixels.
Finally, edit your photos carefully. Digital photos are easy to change, but don't overdo it! Some people love black and white photos because they look classic. Others prefer posed group photos. A quick snapshot can also capture a special moment. Put your best photo in a frame, or share it online with a good caption. And remember: press the shutter gently, and keep your lens clean!

Since its invention in the nineteenth century, photography has been seen as a uniquely truthful medium. Unlike a painting, a photograph seemed to record reality exactly as it was. Early photographers spent hours in the darkroom, carefully controlling the exposure as they developed each image by hand.
In the twentieth century, photojournalism transformed how people understood the world. Powerful images of war, famine and protest shaped public opinion in ways that written reports rarely could. Yet even these photographs were never entirely objective. Every photographer makes choices about composition, deciding what to include and what to leave outside the frame, and a candid moment can tell a very different story from a carefully arranged scene.
Today, with high-resolution cameras in every pocket and powerful editing software, the relationship between photography and truth has become even more complex. Images can be altered so easily that viewers must question whether what they see actually happened. At the same time, the sheer number of photos raises legal questions: many people share images online without realising that they are protected by copyright.
Despite these challenges, photography remains an art of seeing. Professional photographers still wait patiently for the golden hour, when soft light transforms ordinary scenes, or for the perfect silhouette against the evening sky. They adjust the aperture and shutter speed to control light and depth. Technology has changed the tools, but the essential skill, noticing what others overlook, remains the same.
